activities.caption: walk the three classic answers to the mind–body problem
activities.name: cgsFunctionBranch

config.root: You are asked: what is the relation between mind and matter? Walk the classic answers.

start.text: Descartes' seventeenth-century move starts the problem. What do you say?

choices.label: Two distinct substances, interacting in the pineal gland
choices.feedback: Dualism — sharp, influential, and still every everyday theory of mind; but the interaction remains mysterious.

choices.label: The mental IS the physical
choices.feedback: Physicalism — almost all scientists' assumption; now the qualia question bites: why does it feel like anything at all?

physicalism.text: If the mental is the physical, why is there experience? Chalmers (1995) calls this the hard problem — the field's honest boundary.

choices.label: Define mental states by what they do, not what they are made of
choices.feedback: Functionalism — the field's licence: the same role could be played by neurons, silicon or water pipes.

dualism.text: Dualism bequeathed the problem's shape; cognitive science instead studies what mind does — leaving the hard problem honestly open.

functionalism.text: Functionalism: mind is organisation rather than substance — so minds can be studied, built and compared across substrates.

config.why: Dualism, physicalism and functionalism are the classic answers; the hard problem of experience is the honest leftover.

activities.anchor: It is a behavioural criterion, not a metaphysical one
activities.caption: true or false — what the Turing test settles
activities.name: cgsTuringJudge

statements.s: A machine that passes the Turing test has been shown to think.
statements.why: Passing establishes indistinguishable responses and leaves Searle's question standing: does fluent symbol-manipulation amount to understanding?

statements.s: Turing's move was to replace 'can machines think?' with a test you can actually administer.
statements.why: Can its behaviour be told apart from a human's? — the operational spirit of 1950.

statements.s: Searle's Chinese Room grants that passing tests establishes understanding.
statements.why: It is the standing objection: symbol-manipulation that passes tests might still lack understanding.

statements.s: The argument between Turing and Searle remains refined but unresolved.
statements.why: The field's oldest running experiment — a marker of what behaviour can settle, not a closing score.

activities.anchor: rats allowed to explore a maze with no food reward caught up almost at once
activities.caption: fill the blanks — what the latencies revealed
activities.name: cgsMapCloze

config.text: Tolman argued they had formed a %%0%% — an inner picture of the layout — not a chained series of left-right turns. Rewarded %%1%% in training, they improve almost immediately; having watched a shorter route, they %%2%% it when the usual path is blocked.
config.hint: The latencies say otherwise: learning happened without the prize.

activities.caption: call the cost of one more turn
activities.name: cgsRotateEst

config.prompt: Shepard and Metzler (1971) rotated paired 3-D shapes and timed decisions. Roughly what does one additional 60-degree turn cost?
config.why: About a second per 60 degrees — as if the image were turned at a constant rate and compared when the angles matched.
config.context: A decade-long debate about whether imagery is truly picture-like followed — and a template for how the field argues.

activities.anchor: Any information-processing system can be explained at three levels
activities.caption: pair each story of one memory with its question
activities.name: cgsMarrMatch

config.prompt: Why did you remember your password? Pair each account with its question:

pairs.right: what problem is it solving, and why?
what representations and steps does it use?
what physical machinery runs those steps?
implementation mistaken for algorithm — the classic level-crossing error

config.why: Software, program and hardware: knowing the transistors does not give you the spreadsheet — but both, at their own level, are exact.

activities.anchor: Each grammar captured something and missed something
activities.caption: file each result under the grammar that produced it
activities.name: cgsGrammarSort

config.prompt: File each result under the grammar that produced it:

items.label: production systems — rules over symbols — reproducing human errors
networks learning their own weights, making the same past-tense mistakes children make
perception formalised as optimal inference under uncertainty
the General Problem Solver, evaluated against human protocols line by line
the tradition that scaled up decades later into deep learning
the mind as an inference engine updating prior beliefs with evidence

config.why: Which representations, what learning, how much is innate — the argument between them is the field's productive engine.

activities.caption: put the revolution's landmarks in order
activities.name: cgs1956Order

config.prompt: The cognitive revolution assembled piece by piece — put the landmarks in order:
items: The fifty-year ban: mind-talk banished, only observable behaviour studied
George Miller's magic number seven — mental processes as measurable quantities
Chomsky's assault, completed by his 1959 review of Skinner
Institutions arrive — the Cognitive Science journal (1977) and Society (1979)
config.why: Less a discovery than a permission slip: to talk about representations again, with methods.
